methodological_rigor.justification: The study leverages two large, complementary resources (~440,000 individuals from UK Biobank and Viking Genes, plus 63.6 million NHS DigiTrials records) with clear cohort descriptions, rigorous QC pipelines for genotype/exome data (including removal of sex mismatches, heterozygosity filters, relatedness pruning with KING), and validation of pathogenic genotypes via Taqman and Sanger sequencing. Regional assignment and Irish ancestry clustering via IBD + Leiden community detection, anchored with external reference panels (Irish DNA Atlas, People of the British Isles, Trinity Student dataset), are methodologically appropriate. Limitations acknowledged include healthy-volunteer bias in UKB and assumed uniform penetrance across regions. Statistical handling is adequate (Hardy-Weinberg tests, one-sided chi-squared with explicit statistics and p-values, correlation reporting) but lacks multiplicity correction across 29 regions and 42 ICBs, no confidence intervals on predicted genotype frequencies/ratios, and no formal sensitivity analysis for the genetic-risk-to-prevalence ratio calculations.

clinical_relevance_loe.justification: This is a descriptive population-cohort/EHR cross-sectional analysis using UK Biobank and NHS DigiTrials, consistent with Oxford LoE 2b (individual cohort study). Clinical relevance is direct and actionable: the manuscript maps regions of highest genetic risk (Northwest Irish, Outer Hebrides) and identifies likely under-diagnosis areas (Birmingham, North Cumbria, Northumberland, Durham), explicitly informing where community screening programs and health-economic modelling should be prioritized. Findings link to the ACMG SF v3.0 inclusion of HFE p.Cys282Tyr and an existing actionable return-of-results workflow in Viking Genes. While oncology relevance (hepatocellular carcinoma prevention via early venesection) is present but secondary to iron-overload morbidity broadly, the translational path to screening policy is concrete rather than speculative.

reporting_quality.justification: As an observational cohort/cross-sectional study, STROBE is the applicable standard; the manuscript covers background/rationale, cohort definitions, variables, data sources, QC, statistical methods, and limitations in a structured way, with a Nature Portfolio Reporting Summary referenced. Tables 1-4 and Fig. 1 clearly present results with denominators, MAC/MAF, and prevalence. Gaps include no explicit flow diagram of participant inclusion/exclusion, limited discussion of missing data handling in DigiTrials beyond the Unknown ethnicity group, and no pre-registration. Data availability is moderate: UKB and NHS DigiTrials are accessible via approved applications (project IDs provided), Viking Genes protocols cite prior publications, ClinVar and allele-frequency-browser sources are named, but no explicit code/script repository is mentioned and links in the provided text are redacted, so reproducibility relies on reconstructing pipelines from described tool versions (PLINK v2, Eagle 2.4.1, hap-ibd, leidenalg 0.10.2, R 4.4.2).

novelty_literature.justification: The study provides the first systematic 29-region landscape of HFE p.Cys282Tyr and p.His63Asp across the British Isles and Ireland and the first integration of large-scale genetic risk with NHS DigiTrials-level clinical diagnosis prevalence (63M records) to identify under-diagnosis hotspots. Novel granular findings include Northwest Irish and Outer Hebridean maxima, the Ulster Scots vs indigenous Irish genetic structure in Northern Ireland, and the East Asian SLC40A1 p.Ser209Leu observation potentially explaining Chinese haemochromatosis prevalence. However, the core epidemiological signal (HFE variant frequency highest in Celtic-ancestry populations, Irish predominance) confirms long-established knowledge, and penetrance estimates used are imported from Lucas et al. 2024. The contribution is a meaningful extension/high-resolution geographic mapping rather than a first-in-class or paradigm-shifting discovery.

writing_presentation.justification: The manuscript is well organized with clear Introduction-Methods-Results-Discussion flow, precise numerical reporting, and coherent narrative linking genetic risk to diagnostic prevalence to screening implications. Tables 1-4 effectively condense multi-population frequency and regional prevalence data, and Fig. 1 provides an intuitive cartographic summary. Language is generally crisp and scientifically calibrated (e.g., distinguishing predicted vs observed homozygote counts, noting E83.1 coding caveats). Minor issues: some embedded table text is dense and would benefit from clearer column separation in the Table 1 rendering, and the Discussion occasionally drifts into historical/speculative territory (Norse/Anglo-Saxon dilution, Ulster Plantation) that, while interesting, is untested in this paper.

key_strengths: Very large combined sample (~440,000 genotyped individuals plus 63.6M NHS DigiTrials records) with appropriate QC, validation (Taqman, Sanger) and cross-cohort integration
Fine-grained 29-region mapping and IBD/Leiden-based identification of Ulster Scots vs indigenous Northwest Irish clusters with anchoring to external reference panels
Actionable linkage of genetic risk to NHS diagnosis prevalence, identifying specific under-diagnosed regions (Birmingham, North Cumbria, Northumberland, Durham) with direct screening-policy relevance
Clear STROBE-consistent reporting with tool versions, project IDs, and acknowledgement of UKB healthy-volunteer bias and uniform-penetrance assumption
key_concerns: No multiplicity correction despite dozens of pairwise regional chi-squared comparisons, and no confidence intervals on predicted homozygote frequencies or genetic-risk-to-prevalence ratios
Penetrance estimates (0.56 and 0.06) are imported from a single prior UKB study (Lucas et al. 2024) and assumed uniform across regions; sensitivity analyses for this assumption are absent

DigiTrials E83.1 coding may conflate genotype-only notification with clinical iron overload (as the authors acknowledge), and the Unknown-ethnicity bias is discussed qualitatively rather than quantified
No explicit participant flow diagram or code repository; reproducibility requires reconstructing pipelines from tool-version citations alone

Core finding of Celtic/Irish enrichment incrementally extends well-established literature; the primary novelty is geographic resolution and EHR linkage rather than mechanistic or paradigm-shifting discovery
chief_reviewer.rationale: Methodologically solid population-genetics/EHR study with clear translational implications for screening policy, strong sample size, and appropriate reporting. Statistical gaps (no multiplicity correction, no CIs) and the incremental nature of the core Celtic-enrichment finding keep it below Tier 1 (Nature Medicine/Lancet Oncology caliber) but comfortably within Tier 2 (e.g., Nature Communications, ESMO Open-type venues), contingent on minor revisions addressing statistical robustness and reproducibility artifacts.
